title: C++ Knowledge Assessment
description: Core C++ knowledge check for a quant developer: the memory model, RAII, smart pointers, move semantics, iterator invalidation, virtual dispatch cost, atomics and memory ordering, undefined behaviour, vtables, STL complexity, templates and value categories. 30 minutes. Code-output questions show self-contained C++17 snippets, read them as the compiler would.

questions.prompt: What does RAII stand for, and what is the core idea?
options: Resource Access In Iterators, resources are freed whenever an iterator is invalidated
Resource Abstraction via Indirect Internals, all resources must be wrapped in virtual interfaces
Resource Acquisition Is Initialisation: constructors acquire resources and destructors release them at scope exit.
Runtime Algorithm and Interface Inheritance, resources are managed by a central runtime allocator
questions.explanation: RAII ties a resource's lifetime (heap memory, file handles, locks, sockets) to an object's lifetime: the constructor acquires, the destructor releases. Because destructors run deterministically on scope exit, including during stack unwinding when an exception fires. RAII makes leaks and dangling handles structurally impossible without try/catch sprinkled everywhere. It is the single most important C++ idiom.

questions.prompt: Which statement about automatic (stack) storage duration is TRUE?
options: Automatic objects require a paired new expression on every path
Automatic objects persist until explicit delete after their scope
Automatic objects end their lifetimes when their scope exits
Automatic objects are always garbage-collected after their last use
questions.explanation: Automatic storage duration ties lifetime to scope exit, including exception unwinding for fully constructed objects. The standard does not require a specific stack-pointer instruction or garbage collector.

questions.prompt: What does shared_ptr add over unique_ptr, and at what cost?
options: Copy semantics only: copies share the same deleter but each pointer keeps its own private count
Shared ownership uses a control block and reference counting; the object dies when its last owning shared_ptr is released.
Nothing, they are interchangeable, shared_ptr is merely the older API
Shared ownership via a per-object spinlock: the object is destroyed when the FIRST owner goes away
questions.explanation: shared_ptr tracks shared ownership through a control block, with reference-counting overhead. Implementations support the required thread-safety of separate shared_ptr objects, but the pointee is not thereby made thread-safe. unique_ptr instead expresses exclusive ownership.

questions.prompt: C++ Knowledge Assessment: trace cpp-q4 and give the exact printed output.
questions.explanation: Constructing s prints ctor. take(s) passes an lvalue by value, so the copy constructor builds the parameter. take(std::move(s)) casts s to an rvalue reference, so overload resolution selects the move constructor. The key insight: std::move moves nothing, it is just a static_cast to rvalue that changes which constructor is chosen.

questions.prompt: Which statement about iterator invalidation is correct?
options: Vector reallocation invalidates references, pointers and iterators
Map insertion invalidates all old iterators because nodes rebalance
Vector reallocation preserves iterators but invalidates only values
List erasure invalidates all iterators even to surviving elements
questions.explanation: Vector reallocation moves elements into new storage and invalidates pointers, references and iterators. List erasure invalidates those to erased elements, while map insertion does not invalidate existing iterators.

questions.prompt: What is the main recurring cost of a virtual function call compared to a direct (non-virtual) call?
options: Every virtual call allocates a new object on the dynamic heap
An unresolved virtual target adds indirect dispatch and may limit inlining
Every virtual call locks a shared table before invoking the function
A system call schedules another thread for each virtual dispatch
questions.explanation: An indirect virtual call can add dispatch and branch-prediction costs, but the optimiser may prove the target and devirtualise it. Neither a universal fixed cost nor permanent inability to inline is a C++ language guarantee.

questions.prompt: What does memory_order_relaxed on an atomic fetch_add guarantee?
options: Atomicity for that variable without ordering surrounding operations
Automatic release-acquire synchronisation with all other variables
Plain non-atomic increment with only a compiler optimisation barrier
Full sequential consistency for every memory access in every thread
questions.explanation: Relaxed operations preserve atomicity and the atomic object's modification order. They do not create release-acquire ordering for unrelated surrounding accesses; confusing those guarantees can introduce data races.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are undefined behaviour in standard C++? Select all that apply.
options: Incrementing an unsigned int past its maximum value
Overflowing a signed int
Reading v[10] on a std::vector<int> of size 5 with operator[]
Reading the value of an automatic int variable that was never initialised
questions.explanation: Unsigned arithmetic is defined: it computes modulo $2^n$ and wraps. Signed overflow, out-of-bounds access, and reading an indeterminate value are all UB, the standard places no constraints on behaviour, so the compiler may assume they never happen and optimise accordingly (which is why UB can produce bizarre, delayed, or 'impossible' symptoms far from the bug).

questions.prompt: In a common C++ ABI, what do a vptr and vtable do, and why is exactly one vptr per polymorphic object not a portable rule?
questions.modelAnswer: A vptr is an implementation mechanism pointing to virtual-dispatch metadata. Multiple inheritance can require multiple vptrs or tables in common ABIs, and the C++ standard does not mandate either representation.
questions.explanation: The C++ language specifies virtual dispatch behaviour, not a required vtable layout. Common ABIs often use one vptr in simple single inheritance, while multiple inheritance can add more. Exactly one per object is therefore not a portable claim.

questions.prompt: Which pairing of lookup complexity is correct?
options: unordered_map: average O(n); map: always O(1)
unordered_map: average O(1), worst O(n); map: O(log n)
unordered_map: worst O(1) always; map: average O(1)
unordered_map: always O(log n); map: always O(n)
questions.explanation: The standard specifies complexity contracts rather than requiring a red-black-tree implementation. Hash lookup can degrade under collisions, whereas map has logarithmic lookup complexity.

questions.prompt: C++ Knowledge Assessment: trace cpp-q11 and give the exact printed output.
questions.explanation: The compiler instantiates the template twice from the same source: twice<int> returns $5 + 5 = 10$, and twice<double> returns $5.0$, which streams as '5'. Templates are a compile-time code generator, one definition, one machine-code body per set of template arguments, which is why template code lives in headers and why type errors surface at instantiation time.

questions.prompt: Given `int x = 3;`, which of these expressions is an rvalue?
options: x
x = 5 (the assignment expression itself)
questions.explanation: x names a stored object, so it is an lvalue, and so are the other two traps: built-in assignment yields the assigned-to object ($x = 5$ is an lvalue referring to x), and pre-increment ++x also yields x as an lvalue. Only $x + 1$ produces a temporary value with no identity: a prvalue, which is an rvalue. (Post-increment x++ is also a prvalue, it yields a copy of the old value.) Value categories decide what std::move, perfect forwarding and overload resolution do, so this vocabulary is not academic.
